doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: No music in Italian schools; brother's band and saxophone
summary: Italian schools lack music; she moved from piano to sax to join her brother's blues band, and describes her supportive travelling parents.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did your parents understand when you embraced jazz as a — I’ll use the word “passion.” Was it a passion for you in high school?

Well we don’t ever, you know in Italy everybody’s kind of thinking that you know it’s a country all the belle canto, the music and the conservatory, the opera — so there has to be music at school. And as a matter of fact it’s absolutely not like that. In elementary school we have recorder and choir. In middle school we have the history of music but not actual practicing instruments or anything. And in high school we don’t have music. So there’s absolutely no music at school. And unless you have parents that are, you know, willing to enroll you in some extracurriculum outside of the school music course you are not exposed to music. I was lucky that my grandmother played piano and, you know, so

somehow I started, through piano I started kind of experimenting, kind of like pop and then my brother started to play guitar, he put the band together and it was a blues band then he convinced me that if I — he wanted a horn section. He convinced me that if I played saxophone I would be popular with boys. So that’s the only reason I went into music.
Of course. I find a husband. I highly suggest it for any single out there to pick up an instrument.
Well there you go. You know because later I was going to ask you about advice to up and coming musicians so you could put that on the list.

But you know my parents, they — I have an unusual set of parents. You know they travel all over the world, not the classical Italian parents if somebody can think — my mother all over the world. So one thing they taught me is just like you have wings, use it. So the freedom, and knowing people, knowing culture just enlarges your mind and grows your heart. So that was the best supporting environment I ever had, and I’m lucky for that.
